rationale.d: COP improvement is negligible (~3%); VRF part-load advantage is marketing hype; Philippine climate lacks sufficient seasonal variation to benefit from modulation.
rationale.correct: Step 1: Design condition COP = 3.8 (33°C outdoor, 100% load). Step 2: Part-load condition COP = 4.6 (28°C outdoor, 40% load). Step 3: COP improvement = (4.6 − 3.8) ÷ 3.8 × 100% = 0.8 ÷ 3.8 × 100% = 21.1% ≈ 21% COP gain. Why matters: Philippine climate 70–90% RH year-round with outdoor temps ranging 25–34°C. Systems operate at <100% load ~70–80% of the year (cool months May–Oct, intermittent peak loads). This part-load COP advantage (21% in this scenario) compounds across the 8–10 month cooler season, delivering 15–20% average annual energy savings vs. systems with flat COP (split-type, package units). For 80 TR system at 3.8 COP design, annual energy consumption assuming 60% average seasonal load factor, 2,500 operating hrs/year: Output 80 TR × 12,000 × 0.6 × 2,500 hr = 1,440 million BTU/yr = 422 MWh; Input 422 ÷ 4.0 (blended seasonal COP, account 30% time at full-load 3.8 COP + 70% part-load 4.3 COP average) ≈ 105.5 MWh/yr vs. flat-COP system 422 ÷ 3.8 = 111 MWh/yr. Savings ≈ 5.5 MWh/yr × ₱12,500/MWh = ₱68,750/year. Over 8-year payback horizon, VRF capital premium (~₱48,000/TR vs. ₱35,000/TR = ₱1.04M additional) recovers via cumulative energy savings. Source: ALE-UTIL-002-04 VRF Systems section; ASHRAE part-load performance data; tropical seasonal operation patterns.
rationale.takeaway: VRF part-load efficiency gain (15–25% vs. design condition) is substantial and materializes across 6–8 cooler months in tropical Philippines; this seasonal compounding is primary driver of VRF life-cycle cost advantage over fixed-COP systems (split, package, chiller operating at constant capacity).
